subtitle: Practice naming a direction as a result for the people served, choosing priorities with clear criteria, explaining the why to your teams and checking who is better off, so you can see who benefits first and who waits.
audience: For managers of managers, deputy and assistant directors and senior leaders who set priorities across teams in human services and disability services. Program leads who shape a direction across several units will also find it useful.

lessons.title: Naming a direction as a result for people
objectives: Write a result statement that names a population, a place and a condition of well-being for people your teams serve.
Distinguish the whole population from the program population your teams reach directly.
Describe your teams' contribution to the result in one plain sentence.
Identify who is furthest from the result now and how you would learn from them.
lessons.teaching:
Direction is easiest to follow when it names a change in people's lives. Many leaders state direction as activity: finish the redesign, modernize the system, clear the backlog. Those may be the right tasks, but they describe what staff will do, not what should be different for the people served. It is worth asking where you learned to state direction that way. For many of us it came from work plans and status reports, which count tasks because tasks are easy to count.

Results Count offers a plain structure for stating a direction as a result. The approach, developed by the Annie E. Casey Foundation, has leaders write a result statement that names a population, a place and a condition of well-being that every member of that population should be able to experience, for example, all adults receiving disability services in a region have a real choice about where they live. Casey also separates the whole population from the program population, the part of it that a particular service is meant to reach. Most teams influence the program population directly and the whole population only together with partners, which is why the next step matters.

Your teams' contribution is the honest middle ground between the result and the task list. Write one sentence for the result and one for what your teams will add to it. Then ask who within the population is furthest from that result today, and whose experience is missing from how you know. Casey's guide asks leaders to stay aware of who is most disadvantaged in reaching the result. Finding out usually means asking people served, self-advocates, families and county or lead agency partners before the direction is fixed, not after.

A result statement gives every later choice a test. The Government Alliance on Race and Equity's Racial Equity Toolkit separates results in the community from outcomes inside the organization. It uses three performance questions from Results-Based Accountability, developed by Mark Friedman: how much did we do, how well did we do it, and is anyone better off? When a priority cannot be linked to someone being better off, that does not make it wrong. It means you should be able to explain why it comes first.
lessons.keyPoint: Direction names what should be different for people, not only what staff will do. State the result, say what your teams contribute to it, and learn who is furthest from it before the direction is fixed.
lessons.example: Practice case: Rosalind, a deputy director in disability services, is drafting next year's direction for four teams that support waiver programs. Her draft lists three goals: finish the case management system upgrade, reduce the backlog of service plan reviews and update provider guidance. Tomasz, one of her managers, asks what the three goals add up to for people receiving services. The plan goes to the division's leadership team in two weeks.
lessons.question: What should Rosalind do with her draft?
choices: Keep the three goals as written, since each is concrete and measurable, and add an opening line saying that all three serve people receiving services.
Replace the three goals with a broad vision about independence and choice, so that each team can decide for itself how best to contribute to it.
Write a result for people served and a contribution line for her teams, test both with self-advocates and lead agencies, then keep the goals that fit.
feedback: Concrete goals help, but a general line does not show which result they serve or who benefits first. Teams could finish all three and still not know whether anyone is better off.
A vision invites ownership, but without a named result and contribution, teams fill the gap with their own defaults, and the people furthest from the result can stay out of view.
This is the strongest choice. It keeps the useful tasks, ties them to a result people would recognize, and checks the wording with people who live it before the plan is fixed.
lessons.reflection: When you describe your area's direction, do you usually start with tasks or with what should be different for people? Where did you learn that habit?
lessons.action: For one area you lead, write two sentences: the result you want for a population you serve, and what your teams contribute to it. Read them to a partner outside your teams and ask what they would expect to see change.

check.question: Which of these is a result, as the Results Count approach describes one, rather than an activity?
check.correct: Adults with disabilities in the county who want paid work have a job that fits their goals.
wrong: The division completes its case management system upgrade on schedule and on budget this year.
Every team reviews its service plan backlog and reports its progress each month.
check.feedback: A result names a population, a place and a condition of well-being that people should experience. An upgrade or a backlog review may help reach it, but each describes what staff do, not what is different for people.

lessons.title: Choosing what comes first and who waits
objectives: Apply a short, shared set of criteria to compare competing priorities before choosing.
Identify who benefits first and who bears the cost of waiting under each option.
Compare Minimization, Acceptance and Adaptation habits in the way a team sets priorities.
Plan interim support or a firm date for work that is deferred.
lessons.teaching:
Every priority list is also a waiting list. When you choose what comes first, you also choose whose needs wait, for how long and with what support in the meantime. Leaders rarely say that part out loud, and a plan that lists only what was chosen hides the second list. Naming it is not a reason to avoid choosing. Naming it is how you choose with your eyes open.

Clear criteria make a choice easier to explain and easier to challenge. Minnesota's Step-by-Step Guide for the State Equity Analysis Tool suggests ranking recommendations by their likely impact and how feasible they are to carry out. Casey's Results Count guide adds strategy criteria, among them being informed by data, working at more than one level, being actionable with capacity that exists or can be built, and having a real chance of moving the result for the whole population. Agree on a short set before you compare options, so the criteria are not chosen to fit a favorite.

The equity question sits inside the tradeoff: who benefits first from what we chose to do first, and who waits? The GARE toolkit asks who will benefit from or be burdened by a decision, and says the earlier those questions are asked, the better. Casey's guide asks whether a strategy worsens or ignores existing disparities, and how you know. Look closely at who carries the cost of delay. A project that waits a year may cost one group little and another group a great deal, often the people who already had the least access. Ask the people who would wait what the delay would mean for them.

The same skill can be practiced in different ways along the intercultural development continuum. A Minimization habit sounds fair: start with whatever is most ready, and take the rest in the order it arrived. An Acceptance habit notices that readiness often reflects who already had staff time, funding or relationships, and that first-come order can repeat that pattern. An Adaptation habit changes the method: the team scores options against shared criteria, asks who bears the wait, and sets interim support or a firm date for what is deferred. These describe routines, not people, and any team can move between them.
lessons.keyPoint: Every priority list is also a waiting list. Agree on criteria first, ask who benefits first and who waits, and give deferred work a date or interim support instead of an open-ended delay.
lessons.example: Practice case: Deshawn manages three supervisors in an economic assistance area and has staff time for one major project this year. One option updates an online application that most people already use without trouble. The other rebuilds the phone and in-person help used mostly by older adults and people with limited English. The online update is ready to start, with a vendor in place. Mei, one of his supervisors, says the second will take longer to scope.
lessons.question: How should Deshawn decide which project goes first?
choices: Agree on criteria with his supervisors, compare both projects on impact, feasibility and who waits, and set a date for the one that waits.
Start the online update because it is ready, has a vendor and will show results quickly, then take up the phone and in-person help next year.
Ask each supervisor to rank the two projects, then go with the one most of them favor, so the choice reflects the whole management team.
feedback: This is the strongest choice. It makes the criteria visible, names who carries the delay, and gives the deferred work a real commitment instead of an open-ended wait.
Readiness matters, but choosing by readiness alone can favor the people already best served. Those who rely on phone and in-person help carry another year of the current wait.
A shared vote feels inclusive, but without agreed criteria it reflects whoever is closest to each project, and people who rely on phone and in-person help have no voice in it.
lessons.reflection: Think of a priority you set recently. Which work or which groups of people waited because of it, and how did you learn what the wait cost, if you did?
lessons.action: Pick one choice between two pieces of work you face now. Write three criteria you would use, who benefits first under each option and who would wait, then share the criteria with your supervisors before you decide.

check.question: What does it mean to say that every priority list is also a waiting list?
check.correct: Choosing what goes first also decides whose needs wait, for how long and with what support.
wrong: Priorities are best set by how quickly each project can show visible results.
Work should be taken in the order it arrived so that no group is favored.
check.feedback: Ordering work distributes delay as well as benefit. Speed and arrival order can both look fair, but neither asks who carries the cost of waiting or whether it falls on people who already had the least.

lessons.title: Connecting teams to the direction and inviting challenge
objectives: Explain the result, the criteria and who waits when you share a direction with your teams.
Design a way to invite challenge that offers more than one way to respond.
Draft a one-sentence contribution statement with each supervisor that shows how teams connect.
Distinguish what is open to change from what is already decided, and say so plainly.
lessons.teaching:
Teams carry out a direction better when they understand why it was chosen. Minnesota Management and Budget's Enterprise Leader Competency Definition Guide describes leading the organization as guiding and setting vision across a large team or group of teams. At its most developed level, that includes giving the reasons for a change, monitoring results and changing plans as needed. Explaining the why means sharing the result, the criteria and who waits, not only the decision.

Inviting challenge is part of setting direction, not a threat to it. Supervisors and staff see consequences you cannot see from your seat. Ask what the direction treats as normal, who it might leave out and what you have missed. Give people more than one way to answer: in the meeting, in writing afterward or one to one. Leave time for people who think best after a meeting, and make the materials readable for everyone, including people who use captioning or a screen reader. The same guide places bringing in diverse internal and external views when prioritizing at its most developed level.

Ask each supervisor to say how their team contributes and what they will slow or stop. Casey's Leading for Results report says lasting change takes partners working toward the same result, not one person or organization, and that people can lead from whatever role they hold. One sentence from each supervisor on their team's contribution, and on what will wait to make room, is enough. Write those sentences down where every team can see them. Where two teams' contributions pull against each other, settle it in the open rather than leaving each team to guess.

Listening has to be able to change something. Casey's Race Equity and Inclusion Action Guide distinguishes engagement, which can mean gathering input, from empowerment, where the people affected help make decisions and design solutions. Decide in advance which parts of the direction are open to change, and say so. When a challenge changes the plan, tell people what changed. Changes to duties, workloads or positions that follow from a new direction may involve Human Resources and labor relations, so bring them in before you announce.
lessons.keyPoint: Share the why, not only the decision. Invite challenge in more than one way, say what is open to change, and show people when what they raised changed the plan.
lessons.example: Practice case: Farida, who has low vision and uses a screen reader, manages three supervisors in disability services licensing. She shares the division's direction: faster, clearer licensing reviews so small providers can open and stay open. After the briefing, Kwame, a supervisor, sends a written note: small providers in greater Minnesota were never asked what slows them down. Gustavo says his staff worry the faster timeline means more cases each. Her director expects a plan in a month.
lessons.question: What should Farida do next?
choices: Thank both supervisors, explain that the direction came from division leadership, and ask them to help their teams adjust to the faster timeline this month.
Explain why the direction was chosen, ask small providers what slows them, and check any caseload change with Human Resources and labor relations before announcing it.
Ask her director for two more weeks so she can meet with supervisors and small provider groups and agree on a timeline with them before drafting the plan.
feedback: Naming the source is honest, but it closes the door on two useful challenges. Small providers stay unheard, and staff concerns about workload go unanswered.
This is the strongest choice. Farida shares the why, lets providers' experience shape the plan, and checks any change to workloads with the people who decide it before it is announced.

Taking time to listen is sound, but agreeing on a timeline with everyone first blurs who decides and delays help for small providers. Say what is open to change, listen within the month, and report back.
lessons.reflection: When someone challenges a direction you have shared, what do you feel first? What helps you hear the challenge as information rather than resistance?
lessons.action: Before you next share a priority with your teams, write down what is decided, what is open to change and how people can respond after the meeting. Share all three, and later tell people what you changed because of what you heard.

check.question: A manager invites challenge on a new direction. What makes the invitation real rather than a formality?
check.correct: People know which parts are open to change and later hear what changed because of what they said.
wrong: Everyone gets time to speak in the meeting, and every comment is recorded in the minutes.
The direction is shared well in advance, with a full written account of how it was decided.
check.feedback: Time to speak and advance notice both help, but listening is real only when people know what they can change and see what their challenge changed. Say which parts are open, and report back.

lessons.title: Checking who is better off and changing course openly
objectives: Select at least one measure of who is better off and one of what difference the work made.
Use a group breakdown someone has already prepared to decide whether a direction should be kept, changed or stopped.
Identify ways to report group results without pointing to any individual.
Draft an open update that says what you will keep, change and stop.
lessons.teaching:
A direction is only as good as what you learn from it. Casey's Results Count guide frames performance measures as four questions: who is better off, what difference did we make, how much did we do and how well did we do it? It is easy to report only the last two, because they are the simplest to count. For an assessment queue, the number of assessments completed shows how much was done, while whether people received the services they needed sooner shows who is better off. Choose at least one measure for each of the first two before the work starts, so you are not left judging the direction by effort alone.

Treat a group breakdown as a test of the direction, not only a report. If you are new to reading results by group, other courses in this library on disparity data and on equity measures cover it in depth. Here the question is what the breakdown asks you to decide. Minnesota's Equity Analysis Toolkit asks what the data show about current disparities and needs, broken down by race, gender, disability status, income and other factors. For each group, ask whether the direction is working as intended, working more slowly, or making things worse. Then ask partners which groups your categories do not show well. The GARE toolkit notes that missing data can itself show who has been overlooked.

Breaking results down with care protects people. When a group is small, a table can point to a specific person. Ways to avoid this include combining small groups or several years, reporting a range instead of an exact count, or leaving a cell blank and saying why. Ask your data practices staff which of these your area uses. Measure services, processes and results, never individual staff. Pair the numbers with what people served, families and partners tell you, and ask what a change would look like from where they stand. Casey's Action Guide also cautions against settling for the data that happen to be available instead of the data the question needs.

Changing course openly builds more trust than holding on to a plan that is not working. Minnesota's Step-by-Step Guide asks teams to keep monitoring progress and to be ready to adjust strategies based on evaluation and feedback. Casey's Leading for Results report notes that a trend moving the wrong way is a sign to change the strategy. Treat the change as part of the plan, not as an admission of failure. Say what you learned, what you will keep, what you will change and what you will stop, and who the change will affect.
lessons.keyPoint: Measure who is better off, not only how much was done. Break results down with care, listen beside the numbers, and when the trend is wrong, say what you will keep, change and stop.
lessons.example: Practice case: Ingrid, a deputy director in disability services, set a direction last year to shorten the wait for waiver assessments. The overall wait fell by about a third. When Ayo, a program consultant, breaks the results down with lead agency partners, the gain is mostly in metro counties. In several rural counties the wait grew, and families there say they stopped calling. Ingrid's annual update to the division's leadership team is due in three weeks.
lessons.question: What should Ingrid say in her update?
choices: Report the overall gain and the rural increase together, say what she will change for rural counties, and ask lead agencies and families to help shape it.
Report the one-third reduction as the year's main result and look into the rural counties quietly, so that a partial success keeps the support it needs.
Hold the update until the rural numbers are fully explained, since an incomplete picture could be misread by the leadership team.
feedback: This is the strongest choice. It keeps the real gain, names who is not yet better off, and invites the people closest to the rural wait to help decide what changes.
Protecting support is understandable, but reporting only the total hides that rural families are worse off. A quiet fix also leaves partners unsure whether anyone noticed.
Wanting a full explanation is careful, but waiting delays a change for families already waiting longer. A partial picture, labeled as partial, is more useful than silence.
lessons.reflection: When a result you championed turned out uneven, what made it hard to say so? What would make it easier the next time?
lessons.action: Choose one direction you set this year. Write one measure of who is better off, ask your data staff whether it can be broken down by group without identifying anyone, and draft a short note to your teams on what you will keep, change and stop.

check.question: A direction helped most groups but left one group waiting longer. What makes the leader's update an open change of course?
check.correct: It reports the gain and the gap together and says what will be kept, changed and stopped.
wrong: It leads with the overall gain and notes that the gap is being looked into separately.
It waits until the cause of the gap is fully explained, then reports both together.
check.feedback: An open update keeps the real gain, names who is not yet better off and says what will change. Leading with the total or waiting for a full explanation leaves the people waiting longest out of view.

cards.back: A plain sentence naming a population, a place and a condition of well-being that every member of that population should be able to experience.
The whole population is everyone in a defined group and place. The program population is the part of it that a particular service or team is meant to reach.
What your teams add toward a result that many partners share. It sits between the result and the task list, and it can be measured.
One of three performance questions from Results-Based Accountability. It asks whether people's lives changed, not only how much work was done or how well.
Who bears the delay when other work goes first, for how long and with what support. Every priority list shares it out, whether or not anyone names it.

aid.heading: When you set or restate a direction
items: Write the result as a population, a place and a condition of well-being.
Write one sentence on what your teams contribute to that result.
Ask who is furthest from the result now, and how you know.
Check the wording with people served and partners before it is fixed.

aid.heading: When you choose what comes first
items: Agree on a short set of criteria before comparing options.
Compare each option on likely impact and feasibility.
Ask who benefits first and who bears the cost of waiting.
Give deferred work a date or interim support, and say so.
Bring changes to duties, workloads or positions to Human Resources and labor relations first.

aid.heading: When you check and adjust
items: Track who is better off and what difference was made, not only effort.
Break results down by group and report so that no one can be identified.
Hear from people served, families and partners alongside the numbers.
Say openly what you will keep, change and stop, and who is affected.

sources.title: Annie E. Casey Foundation, Introduction to the Results Count Path to Equity: A Guide to the Accountability for Equitable Results Framework (2019)
sources.note: Supports the result statement, whole and program populations, attention to who is most disadvantaged, the strategy criteria, the disparities question and the four performance questions. US child and family focus; race-specific.

sources.title: Annie E. Casey Foundation, Leading for Results: Developing Talent to Drive Change (2013)
sources.note: Supports that lasting change takes partners aligned on one result, that people can lead from any position, that a wrong-way trend signals a change of strategy, and that Mark Friedman developed Results-Based Accountability. Dated 2013.

sources.title: Annie E. Casey Foundation, Race Equity and Inclusion Action Guide: Embracing Equity, 7 Steps to Advance and Embed Race Equity and Inclusion Within Your Organization (2014)
sources.note: Supports the difference between engagement and empowerment and the caution against using only the data that are available instead of the data needed. Dated 2014 and focused on race; applied here more broadly.

sources.title: Government Alliance on Race and Equity, Racial Equity Toolkit: An Opportunity to Operationalize Equity (2015, updated 2016)
sources.note: Supports results versus organizational outcomes, the three Results-Based Accountability questions, benefit and burden, using the tool early, and the note that missing data can show who has been overlooked. Copy hosted by Cleveland State University.

sources.title: State of Minnesota, Equity Analysis Toolkit: A Quick Guide (June 2024)
sources.note: Supports the questions on breaking data down by race, gender, disability status, income and other factors and on what the data show about disparities and needs. Offered as a tool to adapt to the situation, not as a requirement.

sources.title: State of Minnesota, Step-by-Step Guide: Applying the State of Minnesota Equity Analysis Tool
sources.note: Supports ranking recommendations by likely impact and feasibility, monitoring progress, and being ready to adjust strategies based on evaluation and feedback. Describes good practice, not a mandated procedure.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget, Enterprise Leader Competency Definition Guide
sources.note: Supports the description of leading the organization as setting vision across teams, giving reasons for change, monitoring and adjusting plans, and bringing in diverse views when prioritizing. A competency guide, not a policy.
